title: Travel and transport
objectives: I can buy a bus or plane ticket and ask about schedules, platforms and gates.
I can book a room in a hotel or pousada and ask what is included.
I can choose the right preposition for transport (de ônibus, a pé) and destinations (ir a, ir para, estar em).
I can make polite requests with eu queria and eu gostaria de, and explain why a past form sounds polite.
I can say why each word of this unit is spelled and accented as it is, using the stress rule and the sound rules.
I can describe a past trip combining the preterite and the imperfect.

vocabulary.note:
Usage: the normal word for a bus, plane or boat ticket. It comes from passar, to pass or go through, which is why the literal meaning is passage. Bilhete is used for subway tickets and some others.

Spelling: pas-SA-gem. The ending em predicts stress on the second to last syllable, so no accent is needed. Ss between vowels is the s sound, g before e is the zh sound, and the final em is a nasal diphthong, said like 'ayn' through the nose.

example.target: Comprei a passagem pela internet.
example.source: I bought the ticket on the internet.

vocabulary.note:
Ida is the noun going, made from the verb ir, and volta is return, from voltar. One-way is só ida, literally only going.

Spelling: in volta the l ends the first syllable, so it is said like a w (VOW-ta), as in the sound lesson.

example.target: Eu queria uma passagem de ida e volta.
example.source: I would like a round-trip ticket.
example.source_literal: I wanted a ticket of going and return.

vocabulary.note:
Usage: the station for long-distance buses. It is short for estação rodoviária, where rodoviária is the adjective made from rodovia, highway, in the feminine to agree with estação.

Spelling: ro-do-vi-Á-ri-a. The ending ia counts as two syllables (i and a), so the stress falls on the third to last syllable. No ending predicts that, so an accent is required, and the open a takes the acute.

example.target: O ônibus sai da rodoviária às oito.
example.source: The bus leaves the bus station at eight.

vocabulary.note: Spelling: a-e-ro-POR-to. Two strong vowels (a, e, o) side by side never form a diphthong, so the a and the e are separate syllables. The stress is on the second to last syllable, as the ending o predicts, so no accent is needed.

example.target: Fomos ao aeroporto de táxi.
example.source: We went to the airport by taxi.
example.source_literal: We-went to-the airport of taxi.

vocabulary.note: Spelling: VO-o, two syllables, because two o vowels side by side are two beats. Before the 2009 spelling agreement it was written vôo; the circumflex was removed from words ending in oo. The verb is voar, to fly.

example.target: O voo sai às dez e chega ao meio-dia.
example.source: The flight leaves at ten and arrives at noon.
example.source_literal: The flight leaves at-the ten and arrives at-the half-day.

vocabulary.note:
The opposite is o desembarque. The verb embarcar is built from em-, onto, and barca, boat, which is why it is used for planes too.

Spelling: em-BAR-que. The m after e only nasalizes the vowel, qu before e is a k sound with a silent u, and the final e is said like i. The ending e predicts stress on the second to last syllable, so no accent.

example.target: O embarque começa às dez e vinte.
example.source: Boarding starts at ten twenty.
example.source_literal: The boarding begins at-the ten and twenty.

vocabulary.note:
Bagagem de mão is carry-on luggage, literally luggage of hand.

Spelling: ba-GA-gem. The ending em predicts stress on the second to last syllable, so no accent. The first g comes before a and is the hard g; the second g comes before e and is the zh sound. In mão, the tilde makes the vowel nasal, and the ending ão is stressed on the last syllable by default.

example.target: Pode levar até dez quilos de bagagem de mão.
example.source: You can bring up to ten kilos of carry-on luggage.
example.source_literal: Can take up-to ten kilos of luggage of hand.

vocabulary.note: In the example, pesar, to weigh, has a single s between two vowels, which is said z: PE-za.

example.target: Minha mala pesa vinte e dois quilos.
example.source: My suitcase weighs twenty-two kilos.

vocabulary.note:
Despachar a mala means to hand the suitcase over at the counter so that it travels in the hold. The verb is the same word as English dispatch.

Spelling: des-pa-CHAR. A word ending in r is stressed on the last syllable by default, so no accent. Ch is the sh sound. The s before p ends the first syllable, so it is said s or sh depending on the region.

example.target: Vou despachar uma mala.
example.source: I am going to check one suitcase.
example.source_literal: I-go to-dispatch a suitcase.

vocabulary.note:
Portão is porta, door, plus the suffix -ão, which makes a thing bigger, so the literal meaning is a big door.

Spelling: por-TÃO. The ending ão is stressed on the last syllable by default, so the tilde alone is enough: it makes the vowel nasal and marks the stress. The plural is portões.

example.target: O embarque é no portão doze.
example.source: Boarding is at gate twelve.
example.source_literal: The boarding is in-the gate twelve.

vocabulary.note: Spelling: pas-sa-POR-te. Ss between vowels is the s sound. The ending e predicts stress on the second to last syllable, so no accent. The final e is said like i, so the t before it is said ch: pas-sa-POR-chi.

example.target: Esqueci o passaporte em casa.
example.source: I forgot my passport at home.
example.source_literal: I-forgot the passport in home.

vocabulary.note:
From hora, hour. It is the time at which something is scheduled, or the whole timetable.

Spelling: ho-RÁ-ri-o. The h is silent. The ending io counts as two syllables, so the stress is on the third to last syllable and an accent is required; the a is open, so the acute.

example.target: Qual é o horário do próximo ônibus?
example.source: What time is the next bus?
example.source_literal: Which is the schedule of-the next bus?

vocabulary.note:
A counter or window where you buy a ticket or are served. The word is borrowed from French guichet, which is why its spelling looks unusual.

Spelling: gui-CHÊ. The stress is on the last syllable, but the ending e predicts the second to last, so an accent is written; the e is closed, so the circumflex. Gu before i is the hard g with a silent u, and ch is the sh sound.

example.target: Fui ao guichê comprar a passagem.
example.source: I went to the ticket window to buy the ticket.
example.source_literal: I-went to-the ticket-window to-buy the ticket.

vocabulary.note:
Fazer uma reserva is to make a reservation.

Spelling: re-SER-va. The s between two vowels at the start of the second syllable is said z; the r before the v ends the syllable.

example.target: Fiz a reserva para o feriado.
example.source: I made the reservation for the holiday.

vocabulary.note: Same stem as reserva. Spelling: re-ser-VAR. A word ending in r is stressed on the last syllable by default, so no accent.

example.target: Posso reservar um quarto para duas pessoas?
example.source: Can I book a room for two people?

vocabulary.note:
Usage: the room you sleep in, in a house or a hotel. Quarto de casal, literally room of couple, has a double bed. Quarto de solteiro, literally room of single person, has single beds. The same word also means fourth.

Spelling: QUAR-to. Qu before a is the sound k followed by w, so the u is heard.

example.target: Reservei um quarto de casal.
example.source: I booked a double room.
example.source_literal: I-reserved a room of couple.

vocabulary.note:
Diária is the feminine form of the adjective diário, daily, used as a noun: the daily charge. Hotels price by the day, counted in nights.

Spelling: di-Á-ri-a, the same pattern as rodoviária. The d before the sound i is said j.

example.target: A diária é cento e oitenta reais.
example.source: The nightly rate is one hundred eighty reais.

vocabulary.note:
Usage: a small, often family-run hotel, common at the beach and in small towns. The word comes from pousar, to land, rest or lodge.

Spelling: pou-ZA-da. Ou is a diphthong, a single s between vowels is said z, and the ending a predicts stress on the second to last syllable.

example.target: Ficamos numa pousada perto da praia.
example.source: We stayed at a guesthouse near the beach.
example.source_literal: We-stayed in-a guesthouse near of-the beach.

vocabulary.note:
Agrees with the noun: incluído, incluída. Incluso is a common alternative.

Spelling: in-clu-Í-do. The stress is on the second to last syllable, exactly as the ending o predicts, so the accent is not there to mark stress. It shows that u and i belong to separate syllables, a hiatus. Without it, ui would be read as one diphthong, as in fui.

example.target: O café da manhã está incluído na diária.
example.source: Breakfast is included in the rate.
example.source_literal: The coffee of-the morning is included in-the daily.

vocabulary.note:
Short for metropolitano.

Spelling: me-TRÔ. The word ends in o, which predicts the second to last syllable, but the stress is on the last, so an accent is written; the o is closed, so the circumflex.

example.target: Vou de metrô porque é rápido.
example.source: I go by subway because it is fast.
example.source_literal: I-go of subway because is fast.

vocabulary.note:
Usage: a subway or train station. The long-distance bus station is a rodoviária.

Spelling: es-ta-ÇÃO. The cedilla writes the s sound before a. The ending ão is stressed on the last syllable by default, so the tilde alone marks the nasal sound and the stress. The plural is estações.

example.target: A estação fica a dois quarteirões daqui.
example.source: The station is two blocks from here.
example.source_literal: The station stays at two blocks from-here.

vocabulary.note:
Pegar, literally to grab, is the everyday verb for catching or taking a vehicle: pegar um táxi, pegar o ônibus.

Spelling: TÁ-xi. The ending i predicts stress on the last syllable, but this word is stressed on the first, so it is marked; the a is open, so the acute. The x is said ks here.

example.target: Peguei um táxi até o aeroporto.
example.source: I took a taxi to the airport.
example.source_literal: I-grabbed a taxi until the airport.

vocabulary.note:
Usage: a change from one line or vehicle to another; fazer baldeação is to transfer. The word comes from balde, bucket, the old picture of pouring something from one container into another.

Spelling: bal-de-a-ÇÃO. The l ends the first syllable, so it is said w. The e and the a are two strong vowels and so two syllables. The cedilla writes the s sound before a, and the ending ão is stressed on the last syllable by default.

example.target: Fiz baldeação na estação Sé.
example.source: I changed lines at Sé station.
example.source_literal: I-made transfer in-the station Sé.

vocabulary.note:
Usage: a poltrona is an armchair, and the word is used for the individual seats on buses, planes and in theaters. A cadeira is a plain chair.

Spelling: pol-TRO-na. The l ends the first syllable, so it is said w: pow-TRO-na. The stress is on the second to last syllable, as the ending a predicts, so no accent even though the o is closed.

example.target: Minha poltrona é a vinte e dois, na janela.
example.source: My seat is number twenty-two, by the window.
example.source_literal: My armchair is the twenty and two, in-the window.

vocabulary.note:
Demorar means to delay or to take a long time. With a length of time it says how long something lasts: A viagem demora seis horas. On its own it means to be slow: Não demora means it will not be long.

Spelling: de-mo-RAR. A word ending in r is stressed on the last syllable, so no accent.

example.target: A viagem demora seis horas.
example.source: The trip takes six hours.
example.source_literal: The trip delays six hours.

vocabulary.note:
From passear, to go for a stroll, a walk or a ride. A passeio can be a walk, a drive, a boat trip or a tour.

Spelling: pas-SEI-o. Ss is the s sound and ei is a diphthong, one beat.

example.target: Fizemos um passeio de barco lindo.
example.source: We took a beautiful boat trip.
example.source_literal: We-made a stroll of boat beautiful.

dialogues.title: At the bus station
dialogues.context: Juliana buys a ticket to Belo Horizonte at the ticket window of the rodoviária.

lines.speaker: Juliana
lines.target: Boa tarde. Eu queria uma passagem pra Belo Horizonte, por favor.
lines.source: Good afternoon. I would like a ticket to Belo Horizonte, please.
lines.source_literal: Good afternoon. I wanted a passage for Belo Horizonte, for favor.

lines.speaker: Sérgio
lines.target: Pra quando?
lines.source: For when?

lines.speaker: Juliana
lines.target: Pra amanhã, de manhã. Só ida.
lines.source: For tomorrow morning. One way.
lines.source_literal: For tomorrow, of morning. Only going.

lines.speaker: Sérgio
lines.target: Tem um ônibus às oito e outro às dez. O das oito é convencional e o das dez é leito.
lines.source: There is a bus at eight and another at ten. The eight o'clock one is regular and the ten o'clock one is a sleeper.
lines.source_literal: Has a bus at-the eight and another at-the ten. The of-the eight is conventional and the of-the ten is bed.

lines.speaker: Juliana
lines.target: Quanto tempo demora a viagem?
lines.source: How long does the trip take?
lines.source_literal: How-much time delays the trip?

lines.speaker: Sérgio
lines.target: Demora umas seis horas. O das oito chega às duas da tarde.
lines.source: It takes about six hours. The eight o'clock one arrives at two in the afternoon.
lines.source_literal: Delays some six hours. The of-the eight arrives at-the two of-the afternoon.

lines.speaker: Juliana
lines.target: Perfeito. Eu fico com o das oito. Quanto custa?
lines.source: Perfect. I will take the eight o'clock one. How much is it?
lines.source_literal: Perfect. I stay with the of-the eight. How-much costs?

lines.speaker: Sérgio
lines.target: Cento e vinte reais. Poltrona vinte e dois, na janela.
lines.source: One hundred twenty reais. Seat twenty-two, by the window.
lines.source_literal: Hundred and twenty reais. Armchair twenty and two, in-the window.

lines.speaker: Juliana
lines.target: Pode ser. Posso pagar com Pix?
lines.source: That works. Can I pay with Pix?
lines.source_literal: Can be. Can-I pay with Pix?

lines.speaker: Sérgio
lines.target: Pode sim. O embarque é na plataforma quatro, meia hora antes.
lines.source: You can. Boarding is at platform four, half an hour before.
lines.source_literal: Can yes. The boarding is in-the platform four, half hour before.

dialogues.title: Booking a room
dialogues.context: Henrique phones a pousada to book a room for the holiday weekend.

lines.speaker: Henrique
lines.target: Boa tarde. Eu gostaria de fazer uma reserva para o feriado.
lines.source: Good afternoon. I would like to make a reservation for the holiday.
lines.source_literal: Good afternoon. I would-like of to-make a reservation for the holiday.

lines.speaker: Marta
lines.target: Claro. Para quantas pessoas e quantas noites?
lines.source: Of course. For how many people and how many nights?

lines.speaker: Henrique
lines.target: Para duas pessoas, três noites, a partir de sexta-feira.
lines.source: For two people, three nights, starting on Friday.
lines.source_literal: For two people, three nights, at leaving from Friday.

lines.speaker: Marta
lines.target: Temos um quarto de casal. A diária é cento e oitenta reais, com café da manhã incluído.
lines.source: We have a double room. The rate is one hundred eighty reais per night, with breakfast included.
lines.source_literal: We-have a room of couple. The daily is hundred and eighty reais, with coffee of-the morning included.

lines.speaker: Henrique
lines.target: Fica perto da praia?
lines.source: Is it near the beach?
lines.source_literal: Stays near of-the beach?

lines.speaker: Marta
lines.target: Fica a cinco minutos a pé. A internet é grátis.
lines.source: It is five minutes on foot. The internet is free.
lines.source_literal: Stays at five minutes at foot. The internet is free.

lines.speaker: Henrique
lines.target: Perfeito. A que horas é o check-in?
lines.source: Perfect. What time is check-in?
lines.source_literal: Perfect. At what hours is the check-in?

lines.speaker: Marta
lines.target: A partir das duas da tarde. E o check-out é até o meio-dia.
lines.source: From two in the afternoon. And check-out is until noon.
lines.source_literal: At leaving from-the two of-the afternoon. And the check-out is until the half-day.

lines.speaker: Henrique
lines.target: Posso cancelar a reserva?
lines.source: Can I cancel the reservation?

lines.speaker: Marta
lines.target: Pode, até dois dias antes.
lines.source: Yes, up to two days before.
lines.source_literal: Can, until two days before.

dialogues.title: Checking in at the airport
dialogues.context: Thiago checks in for a flight to Recife and talks to the airline agent, Vera.

lines.speaker: Vera
lines.target: Bom dia. Passaporte ou documento com foto, por favor.
lines.source: Good morning. Passport or photo ID, please.
lines.source_literal: Good day. Passport or document with photo, for favor.

lines.speaker: Thiago
lines.target: Aqui está. Vou despachar uma mala.
lines.source: Here you are. I am going to check one suitcase.
lines.source_literal: Here is. I-go to-dispatch a suitcase.

lines.speaker: Vera
lines.target: A mala pesa vinte e dois quilos. Está dentro do limite. Prefere janela ou corredor?
lines.source: The suitcase weighs twenty-two kilos. It is within the limit. Do you prefer window or aisle?
lines.source_literal: The suitcase weighs twenty and two kilos. Is inside of-the limit. Prefers window or corridor?

lines.speaker: Thiago
lines.target: Janela, por favor. Meu voo está no horário?
lines.source: Window, please. Is my flight on time?
lines.source_literal: Window, for favor. My flight is in-the schedule?

lines.speaker: Vera
lines.target: Está, sim. O embarque começa às dez e vinte no portão doze.
lines.source: Yes, it is. Boarding starts at ten twenty at gate twelve.
lines.source_literal: Is, yes. The boarding begins at-the ten and twenty in-the gate twelve.

lines.speaker: Thiago
lines.target: A que horas o voo chega a Recife?
lines.source: What time does the flight arrive in Recife?
lines.source_literal: At what hours the flight arrives at Recife?

lines.speaker: Vera
lines.target: Chega às duas e quarenta da tarde. Demora três horas e meia.
lines.source: It arrives at two forty in the afternoon. It takes three and a half hours.
lines.source_literal: Arrives at-the two and forty of-the afternoon. Delays three hours and half.

lines.speaker: Thiago
lines.target: Ótimo. E a bagagem de mão?
lines.source: Great. And the carry-on?
lines.source_literal: Great. And the luggage of hand?

lines.speaker: Vera
lines.target: Pode levar até dez quilos. Boa viagem!
lines.source: You can bring up to ten kilos. Have a good trip!
lines.source_literal: Can take up-to ten kilos. Good trip!

grammar.title: Spelling and sound: the words of this unit
grammar.explanation:
Every word in this unit can be read and written with the rules from the first three lessons, and this note shows the rules at work. The method never changes. Divide the word into syllables, find the stressed syllable by ear, read the default from the ending, and compare. The default is this: a word ending in a, e or o (with or without a final s), or in am, em or ens, is stressed on the second to last syllable, and a word ending in anything else is stressed on the last syllable. When the stress disagrees with the default, an accent is written on the stressed vowel: the acute if the vowel is open, the circumflex if it is closed. An accent is never decoration. It says: this word is an exception to the default of its ending.

The stress exceptions in this unit fall into four groups. First, words that end in a, e or o but are stressed on the last syllable: guichê, metrô, café, até, está. The ending predicts the second to last syllable, so the accent is required; the circumflex marks a closed vowel (guichê, metrô) and the acute an open one (café, até, está). The same rule marks stressed one-syllable words that end in e, such as pé, é and Sé, and três, which ends in es. Second, proparoxytones, words stressed on the third to last syllable. No ending predicts that stress, so they always carry an accent: horário, rodoviária, diária, próximo, último, simpática, estávamos. A final ia or io counts as two syllables in this analysis, so horário is ho-RÁ-ri-o. Third, words whose ending predicts the last syllable but which are stressed earlier: táxi and grátis (endings i and is) and incrível (ending l). Fourth, the hiatus accent. A hiatus is two vowels that belong to separate syllables, and an i or u that is stressed and alone in its syllable after another vowel is written í or ú to show the break. In incluído, the stress is already where the ending o predicts, so the accent marks only the hiatus: without it, ui would be read as the single diphthong of fui. Compare gostaria and poderia: the stressed i is also second to last, but it follows a consonant, so nothing needs marking.

Nasal sounds are written in two ways. The tilde makes a or o nasal, and when the word has no other accent it also marks the stress: portão, estação, baldeação, mão, manhã. The ending ão is stressed on the last syllable by default, which is why the tilde alone is enough, and its plural is usually ões: portão and portões, estação and estações, quarteirão and quarteirões. The letters m and n at the end of a syllable are not consonants there; they only nasalize the vowel before them: embarque, cento, vinte, cinco, convencional. The ending em is a nasal diphthong, said like 'ayn' through the nose, and because em predicts the second to last syllable, passagem and bagagem need no accent.

The consonant spellings follow the sound lesson. Ss between vowels is the s sound (passagem, passaporte, passeio, pessoas), while a single s between vowels is z (reserva, pousada, pesa). Ç writes the s sound before a and o (estação, começou), and c is s before e and i (cinco, cedo, convencional). Ch is sh (despachar, guichê, chega). Lh and nh are single sounds, like the li of million and the ny of canyon (melhores, minha). G before r is the hard g (igreja). Qu and gu before e and i are the sounds k and g with a silent u (embarque, quilos, guichê), but before a the u is heard (quarto, quanto). G before e and i is the zh sound, and so is j (passagem, bagagem, janela, Sérgio). H is silent (horário, hora). The letter x has several sounds: ks in táxi and Pix, and s in próximo and before a consonant, as in sexta-feira. An l that ends a syllable is said w (poltrona, baldeação, último, incrível). T and d before the sound i, which includes a weak final e, are said ch and j: passaporte is pas-sa-POR-chi, diária is ji-Á-ri-a, grátis is GRÁ-chis. Verbs ending in gar add a u in the eu form of the preterite to keep the hard g: chegar becomes cheguei and pegar becomes peguei.

Some words keep a spelling the rules do not predict, because they were borrowed. Check-in and check-out are English, said with the English ch. Pix is the name of the Brazilian instant-payment system, said PIKS. Guichê is French. In Thiago, the old-fashioned th is simply t, which becomes ch before the sound i: CHYA-go. Finally, watch for simpática, a false friend, meaning a word that looks like an English word but means something different: it means nice or friendly, not sympathetic.

grammar.title: Prepositions with transport and destinations
grammar.explanation:
A preposition is a short word placed before a noun to say how that noun relates to the rest of the sentence: by, to, at, in, on. English chooses its prepositions for vehicles by habit: you go by bus, sit in a car, ride on a plane, and travel on foot. Portuguese is more systematic. For the means of transport it uses de, whose basic meaning is of or from, followed by the vehicle with no article: de ônibus, de avião, de carro, de trem, de metrô, de táxi, de bicicleta, de Uber. Literally this says of bus, of plane, and it treats the vehicle as a kind of travel, not as one particular object. The everyday exception is on foot, which is a pé, literally at foot; on horseback is a cavalo in the same pattern.

Because de ônibus has no article, it names the means. When you add the article and use em, you name one particular vehicle that you are inside: Vou de ônibus means I go by bus, but Estou no ônibus means I am on the bus, literally in the bus, where no is em plus o. English draws the same line between by bus and on the bus. For the same reason you hear Vou no ônibus das oito, I am taking the eight o'clock bus: the bus is now one specific vehicle.

For where you are heading, Portuguese has two standard prepositions. A means to and marks the point you reach; it is the choice for short trips that you will soon come back from, especially in careful speech and writing: Vou ao banco, Fui à rodoviária. Para means toward or for and looks at the destination as the place you are headed or will stay in, so it is the usual choice for longer trips and for going home: Vou para a Bahia, Vou para casa. The difference is small, and in speech Brazilians use para for almost everything, shortened to pra, with para plus o shortened to pro: Vou pra Bahia, Ele foi pro Rio. In informal speech you also hear em after ir (Vou no mercado), but a and para are what you should write.

Arriving works a little differently. Chegar, to arrive, takes a in careful writing (Cheguei a São Paulo) and em in everyday speech (Cheguei em São Paulo). Both are correct, and em is more natural. Being somewhere always uses em: Moro em Recife, Estou no hotel, Fiquei na pousada. Distance uses a: A estação fica a dois quarteirões daqui, literally stays at two blocks from here, and Fica a cinco minutos a pé, at five minutes on foot.

Some place names carry an article and some do not, and the article decides the contraction. Most cities take none (em São Paulo, em Recife, em Salvador), and so do Portugal and Pernambuco, but Rio de Janeiro does (no Rio, ao Rio), and so do o Brasil, a Bahia and o Ceará (no Brasil, na Bahia, à Bahia). To find out, use the from test: you say Volto de Recife but Volto da Bahia, and the da shows the article. Casa works like a place without an article when it means your own home: Estou em casa, Vou pra casa, Saio de casa. Add a describing phrase and the article returns: Estou na casa da Ana. Trabalho takes the article: Vou ao trabalho, Estou no trabalho. A gente, literally the people, is the everyday word for we, and after a preposition it means us: pra gente is for us.

All the fusions come from the earlier note on contractions: a plus o is ao, a plus a is à (the accent is the crase, the mark that records two a sounds merged into one), em plus o is no, em plus a is na, and para plus o is pro in speech. The crase test from that note works here too: replace the feminine place with a masculine one; if you would say ao, the feminine place takes à. You say Vou ao aeroporto, so you say Vou à rodoviária. No crase appears before a place name without an article (Vou a Recife) or before a verb or a noun used as a fixed phrase (a pé).

grammar.title: Polite requests: eu queria and eu gostaria de
grammar.explanation:
A request is polite when it leaves the other person room to say no. Languages build that room with the same tools: a softer verb, a question instead of a statement, and distance. English says I want a ticket (blunt), I would like a ticket, or I was wondering if I could have a ticket, where the past tense was wondering creates the distance. Portuguese does the same, and the most common everyday softener is eu queria, literally I wanted. It is the imperfect of querer, the tense you met in the imperfect unit, which looks at a state from the inside without saying whether it still holds. I wanted a ticket makes the wish sound like background, not a demand. The present eu quero is not rude, but it is direct, and a stranger behind a counter hears it as abrupt unless you add por favor.

Eu gostaria de is one step more formal. Gostaria is gostar (to like) plus the ending -ia, and it means I would like. A verb form that says what would happen is called the conditional, and the course teaches it fully later; here you only need gostaria and poderia as fixed polite forms. Notice that the -ia is attached to the whole infinitive: gostar plus ia, poder plus ia. The imperfect of an -er verb works differently: it drops the whole infinitive ending -er and adds -ia to what is left, the stem (quer- plus ia is queria, com- plus ia is comia). The two look alike but are built differently: gostaria keeps the full infinitive, while queria is built on the stem. Both are stressed on the i (gos-ta-RI-a, po-de-RI-a), the second to last syllable, so no accent is written.

Both forms work with a noun or with an infinitive: Eu queria uma passagem, Eu queria reservar um quarto. The difference is a preposition. Gostar always needs de (Eu gosto de café), so gostaria de comes before both a noun and an infinitive (Eu gostaria de uma passagem, Eu gostaria de reservar um quarto), while queria takes no preposition.

To ask someone to do something, use Você poderia plus an infinitive, literally you would be able to: Você poderia me dizer onde fica o portão? The small word me means to me. It is a pronoun, a word that stands in for a noun, here the person affected, and in Brazil it sits before the verb it belongs to; a later unit treats these pronouns fully. The simpler everyday version is Pode plus an infinitive: Pode repetir, por favor? Here the subject você is dropped, as Portuguese usually does, and pode is the você form of poder, can. Pode ser, literally can be, is a stock reply meaning that works.

Some small words soften a request too, and each is worth reading literally. Por favor is literally for favor. Com licença is literally with license, in the old sense of permission: you are asking permission to pass or to interrupt, which English renders as excuse me. Desculpa comes from desculpar, to excuse, and is the everyday sorry or excuse me. In shops and snack bars you also hear Me vê plus a noun (Me vê um café), literally me you-see a coffee, meaning get me a coffee, and Vou querer plus a noun (Vou querer um café), literally I-go to-want a coffee, the near future with ir, meaning I'll have a coffee. Both are casual and belong to service situations.

grammar.title: Schedules and duration: sai às, chega às, demora
grammar.explanation:
Portuguese, like English, uses the simple present for scheduled events: O ônibus sai às oito, the bus leaves at eight. To say at a clock time, the preposition is a plus the plural article as, because clock hours are counted as feminine plural words (as oito horas, literally the eight hours, with horas left out). A plus as fuses into às, which is the crase from the earlier note on contractions: O ônibus sai às oito, literally leaves at-the eight. Only one o'clock is singular, so it takes à: à uma. Noon and midnight show the crase test at work. Meio-dia, literally half-day, is masculine because dia is masculine, so you say ao meio-dia. Meia-noite, half-night, is feminine, so you say à meia-noite.

To ask the time of an event, Portuguese says A que horas sai o ônibus?, literally at what hours leaves the bus, with horas plural for the same reason. In casual speech the a is dropped: Que horas o ônibus sai? The part of the day is added with da: duas da tarde, literally two of the afternoon. In printed timetables and announcements you will often see the 24-hour clock instead.

To say how long something takes, Portuguese does not use a verb meaning to take. Demorar literally means to delay or to take a long time, and with a length of time it says how long the trip lasts: A viagem demora seis horas, literally the trip delays six hours. Levar, literally to carry, is the other common verb: Leva três horas de carro, literally carries three hours of car, where de names the means. Durar, to last, also works. Ask Quanto tempo demora? or Quanto tempo leva?, literally how much time delays or carries. In the past the trip has ended, so the preterite is natural: A viagem demorou oito horas. Used alone, demorar means to be slow: Não demora means it will not be long, and Demorou! is what you say to someone who took a long time.

Other words organize a schedule. A partir de means starting from: a plus partir, to leave or depart, plus de, so literally at leaving from. Até means until or up to and does not fuse with the article, so you say até o meio-dia. De hora em hora, literally of hour in hour, means every hour, and a cada vinte minutos, literally at each twenty minutes, means every twenty minutes. Cedo is early. Tarde is late when it is an adverb and afternoon when it is a noun: Chegamos tarde, we arrived late, but à tarde, in the afternoon. To pick one of several, Portuguese drops the repeated noun and keeps the article: o das oito, literally the one of-the eight, means the eight o'clock one, as in o ônibus das oito. A flight is no horário when it is on time, literally in the schedule, and atrasado when it is late, literally set behind, from atrás, behind. The next bus is o próximo ônibus and the last is o último ônibus. For a hotel, O check-in é a partir das duas e o check-out é até o meio-dia.

grammar.title: Narrating a trip: preterite and imperfect together
grammar.explanation:
A travel story is a good place to review the two simple past tenses, because it needs both and shows why. The preterite is the outside view of an action: it happened, it is finished, and it moves the story forward. The imperfect is the inside view: it describes the scene in which the events happen, without saying when anything began or ended. A test: if the answer to And then what happened? is the verb, use the preterite (Chegamos, deixamos as malas, fomos à praia). If the answer to What was it like? is the verb, use the imperfect (Era noite, fazia muito frio, a pousada era pequena, a dona era simpática).

When a long background action is cut off by a short event, the background goes in the imperfect, usually the progressive (estava plus a gerund, the verb form ending in -ndo), and the event goes in the preterite: Estávamos esperando o ônibus quando começou a chover. Começar a plus an infinitive is literally to begin at to rain. Duration follows the same logic. A viagem demorou oito horas presents the trip as a finished whole and so uses the preterite, while A viagem demorava oito horas would describe its usual length, as a habit.

Connecting words show the order of events: primeiro (first), depois (afterwards), em seguida (next, literally in following), mais tarde (later, literally more late), no dia seguinte (the next day, literally in the day following) and por fim (finally, literally by end). Time markers place the trip: no ano passado (last year, literally in the year past), no verão passado, and há dois anos (two years ago). Há is literally there is, so há dois anos is literally there-is two years, and the phrase comes before the time it measures.

The irregular preterite forms most used in trips are in the table: ir and ser share fui and fomos, and fazer gives fiz, ver vi, ter tive, estar estive and trazer trouxe. Foi uma viagem incrível uses the preterite of ser because it judges the whole trip as one completed event, while A comida era deliciosa uses the imperfect because it describes the food as part of the scene. Fomos a pé is the shared form at work: the context a pé tells you it is ir. The adjective simpática is a false friend, a word that looks like an English word but means something else: it means nice or friendly, not sympathetic.

culture.title: Getting around Brazil
culture.text:
Brazil is huge, so how you travel depends a lot on the distance. For long distances many people fly, and the main domestic airlines sell cheap tickets in installments called parcelado, literally parceled. For medium distances and for budget travel, buses are the backbone of the country. Every city has a rodoviária, often a bustling building with ticket counters called guichês. Buses come in different classes: convencional, executivo and leito, a sleeper with reclining seats that is comfortable for overnight trips. Leito is literally bed.

Inside large cities, the metrô is often the fastest option in São Paulo, Rio, Belo Horizonte, Recife, Salvador and Brasília, but it covers only part of the city. Buses are everywhere and the ticket is often paid with an electronic card or Pix. Apps like Uber and 99 are very popular, often cheaper than a táxi, and people say Vou de Uber as naturally as Vou de ônibus, because Uber is treated like any other means of transport. If a friend has a car, pedir carona, literally to ask for a ride, is a common and friendly habit.

For accommodation, besides hotels and hostels you will find pousadas, small guesthouses that often include café da manhã in the rate and are usually run by a family. A woman who runs one is often called Dona followed by her first name, such as Dona Cida; dona means lady or owner and is a respectful title for an older or senior woman. The best-known destinations include the Cristo Redentor, Christ the Redeemer, and the Pão de Açúcar, literally bread of sugar and known in English as Sugarloaf, in Rio. Others are the beaches of Bahia and Pernambuco, the Pantanal, the Amazon, Foz do Iguaçu, Fernando de Noronha and the colonial towns of Minas Gerais such as Ouro Preto, literally Black Gold, named for the gold that made the town rich. Asking locals for dicas, tips, is the best way to find a good restaurant or a hidden beach.

I would like to cancel a room for two people.
I would like to book a room for two people.

exercises.explanation: Demorar (to delay), levar (to carry) and durar (to last) all say how long something takes.

exercises.prompt_source: The bus arrives at two o'clock.
What time does the bus leave?
answers: A que horas sai o ônibus?
A que horas o ônibus sai?
A que horas parte o ônibus?
A que horas o ônibus parte?

exercises.prompt: Word for word, what does 'café da manhã' say?
exercises.explanation: Café is coffee, da is de plus a, and manhã is morning: coffee of the morning, which English calls breakfast.

exercises.hint_source: I arrived in São Paulo at noon.
exercises.explanation: Chegar takes a in careful writing and em in everyday speech.
Being at a place uses em, and em plus o is no.

exercises.prompt_target: A diária custa cento e oitenta reais, café da manhã ___.
exercises.hint_source: The rate is one hundred eighty reais, breakfast included.
exercises.explanation: Incluído agrees with café da manhã, which is masculine.

exercises.audio_target: Fomos de ônibus até a praia.
choices: We went by car to the beach.
We went by bus to the beach.

exercises.prompt_source: We went to the airport by taxi.
answers: Nós fomos ao aeroporto de táxi.
A gente foi ao aeroporto de táxi.
Nós fomos pro aeroporto de táxi.
A gente foi pro aeroporto de táxi.
Nós fomos para o aeroporto de táxi.
A gente foi para o aeroporto de táxi.
Fomos para o aeroporto de táxi.

exercises.hint_source: It was night and it was very cold.
exercises.explanation: Weather and the time of day set the scene, so they use the imperfect.

exercises.prompt: Which form completes the story? Chegamos ao hotel, deixamos as malas e ___ à praia.
exercises.explanation: A step in the sequence of events is a finished action, so it needs the preterite of ir: fomos.

exercises.prompt_source: We arrived late and missed the flight.
How long does the trip take?

exercises.audio_target: O ônibus sai da rodoviária às oito.
exercises.hint_source: The bus leaves the bus station at eight.
